items.body: The US military will on Wednesday detonate some 10,000 pounds of unstable and degraded explosive material in Iowa, where local residents were urged to evacuate amid concerns over possible toxic lead contamination. US officials say the 68 drums of lead azide are at risk of spontaneous explosion. A series of safety measures are being taken to curb potential contamination from the blast, but the Army has encouraged residents of a small town and other nearby areas to leave "out of an abundance of caution."

items.body: November 25th is International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women. The forgotten victims of femicide are the children who find themselves motherless, often because their mother was killed by their own father. Italy recorded 97 female homicides in 2025 – 62 of them were committed by a partner. These crimes leave whole families devastated and children who have to grow up without their parents. FRANCE 24’s correspondent in Italy, Natalia Mendoza, reports.

items.title: Kilmar Ábrego García arrives in Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
items.summary: His deportation to and return from El Salvador became a flashpoint in the debate the US president's immigration agenda.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByRebecka Pieder

Updated 20 minutes ago

Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, is leaving the US for Spain.

He is set to take a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.

His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.

Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."

In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.

"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."

The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.

In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.

The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.

For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.

Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.

After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.

At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

items.title: Russia places Murmansk governor in detention in corruption case
items.summary: Investigators accused Andrei Chibis of embezzling more than one billion rubles (US$12 million) meant to reconstruct a motorway in a mountainous part of the region and build a youth centre, then transferring the funds abroad illegally.
items.body:

World

Russia places Murmansk governor in detention in corruption case

Investigators accused Andrei Chibis of embezzling more than one billion rubles (US$12 million) meant to reconstruct a motorway in a mountainous part of the region and build a youth centre, then transferring the funds abroad illegally.

In this photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Andrei Chibis, the governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region, attends a meeting of the Council for Strategic Development and National Projects at the Kremlin in Moscow on Aug 19, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Pool/Gavriil Grigorov)

MOSCOW: Russia on Wednesday (Nov 25) placed the governor of Murmansk in pre-trial detention on suspicion of large-scale corruption - a rare case of a senior official facing prosecution amid the war in Ukraine.

Andrei Chibis, who has led the strategic Arctic region since 2019, was detained at Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport on Monday as he arrived for a business trip.

Investigators accused the 47-year-old of embezzling more than one billion rubles (US$12 million) meant to reconstruct a motorway in a mountainous part of the region and build a youth centre. They allege he then transferred the funds abroad illegally.

Chibis - who survived an assassination attempt in 2024 - is the first governor to be arrested while in office during Moscow's war against Ukraine.

Moscow's Meshchansky court ruled to keep Chibis in custody for at least two months, pending a trial.

"Investigative procedures are underway. At the moment, there is nothing further to add," the Kremlin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on the case on Wednesday.

Chibis's lawyer, Ruslan Zakaplyuzhny, read out a statement from his client to state media in which he said: "I do not agree with the accusations. I worked honestly and sincerely in the interests of the north. I am confident that, during investigations and in court I will be able to prove my innocence and refute the false accusations."

Chibis is being charged with "embezzlement as part of an organised group" as well as "accepting bribes" of a particularly large sum - crimes punishable by 10 years and 15 years in prison each.

2024 ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT

Russian courts have notoriously low acquittal rates and officials who have fallen foul of the security services and the Kremlin in recent years have been jailed for years.

The Kommersant newspaper reported that during questioning Chibis said he intended to step down voluntarily and join Moscow's forces in Ukraine.

Russia has recruited prisoners en masse for its war effort.

Russian security services began arresting Chibis's associates earlier this year.

The governor's wife Yevgenia Chibis defended him on social media, saying he "genuinely believes in the Murmansk region" and called for the support of locals.

In April 2024, Chibis was stabbed in a knife attack in the Arctic city of Apatity, an extremely rare targeting of an official.

Investigators said the assailant was motivated by a personal dislike. The man - Alexander Bydanov - was sentenced to 13 years in a penal colony. Russian media reported he had been killed in Ukraine earlier this year.

Chibis was appointed to lead Murmansk - a heavily militarised region that is home to Russia's main Arctic port - in 2019.

President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly called to make the strategic development of the region a priority.

items.title: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
items.summary: Odochie rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
items.body:
Image source, peteedochie/Instagram

Image caption,

Pete Edochie was one of Africa's most celebrated film stars

ByWycliffe Muia

Updated 43 minutes ago

Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.

In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.

The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.

Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.

Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.

"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.

The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.

Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.

He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

items.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
items.summary: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers

ByOlga Ivshina, BBC Russian and Yaroslava Kiryukhina, BBC Russian

At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.

BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.

Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.

The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.

Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.

For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.

How we came to a figure near half a million

The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.

We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.

Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.

As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.

Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.

Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.

According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).

Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.

At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.

This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.

The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.

The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.

In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.

Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.

As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.

According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).

Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.

blocks.alt: A portrait of a Russian soldier killed in Ukraine sits on a lamp post in central Maloyaroslavets, 110 km southwest of Moscow, in the Kaluga region

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.

At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.

The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.

Violence in the West Bank, occupied by Israel since 1967, has surged since Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war.

GENEVA: The United Nations (UN) warned on Wednesday (Nov 25) of a growing risk of atrocity crimes being committed by Israel against the Palestinians, and urged all states to take immediate preventative action.

UN rights chief Volker Turk said ongoing Israeli attacks, policies and violations against Palestinians indicated a "widening risk of further atrocity crimes" in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

"Israeli government representatives at highest levels have time and again spelled out policies of annexation, ethnic cleansing and collective punishment in the West Bank," he said in a statement.

"Across society, the incitement to hatred and to perpetration of violations amounting to atrocity crimes - war crimes, crimes against humanity and even genocide - has been appalling."

"I am extremely worried about the increasingly widespread and systematic nature of the violations being perpetrated across both the West Bank and Gaza," Turk said.

"Our warnings have not been heeded, and atrocity crimes continue to recur," said the UN high commissioner for human rights.

"Civilians continue to be killed, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, with senior Israeli officials indicating intent for such displacement to be permanent."

Violence in the West Bank, occupied by Israel since 1967, has surged since Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war.

"All states have the obligation to act, now, to prevent further atrocity crimes against the Palestinians," said Turk.

"There must be independent investigations, and those responsible must be held to account. The work of the international courts in this regard must be supported by all states."

Turk also reminded Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups of their obligations under international law, including to protect civilians and to respect the safety of humanitarian operations.

Trump announces new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China and Singapore

His administration also proposed tariffs on Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders Summit in Shenzhen, China on Nov 18, 2026. (File photo: Reuters/Carlos Barria)

WASHINGTON: United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday (Nov 25) fired a new tariff salvo on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, the European Union and Singapore, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.

His administration proposed new headline tariff rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent, but said duties would be capped at lower levels agreed under trade deals that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

Under the main "Section 301" probe into excess industrial capacity, China would face the highest capped rate of 20 per cent, which would be added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40%, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) said.

Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with Washington, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a Jan 25 public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base.

Washington has long accused China of subsidising industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.

Beijing earlier reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and rejected allegations of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"FALSE ISSUE", CHINA SAYS

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world's top two economies to maintain stable relations.

The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18 per cent for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15 per cent, including existing "Most Favored Nation" duties, for Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the EU and Switzerland.

India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail, the USTR said. Singapore would receive a capped tariff rate of 10 per cent.

Greer told CNBC the proposed caps were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year that also lowered barriers to US exports.

"We're sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said. "So you know we've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in."

Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain under way, Greer said.

Even so, the prospect of new trade barriers weighed on stock markets on Wednesday amid a renewed sell-off in tech stocks. Major US indexes opened down more than 1 per cent, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite down more than 3 per cent.

"It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote.

Separately, the USTR proposed a new 10 per cent tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.

The products were previously exempted from Trump's 25 per cent tariffs on Brazilian goods that were imposed in July. A US official said that despite negotiations, there were "substantial differences" over the allegations.

China warns US against imposing new tariffs

Courtesy for courtesy, curbs for curbs? The two sides of Trump-Xi reciprocity

NEW DUTIES WON'T EXCEED NEGOTIATED LIMITS

Trump's tariffs have contributed to higher prices for US consumers, and a Reuters-Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans' midterm losses found 62 per cent of respondents supported efforts to repeal them.

But Trump has long vowed to restore duties struck down by the US Supreme Court in February. The latest measures follow an eight-month investigation into unfair trade practices under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

Greer said the proposed tariffs would not apply to about US$30 billion of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade.

However, the new duties would be added to tariffs imposed on Chinese goods during Trump's first term, which total roughly 25 per cent.

They would not be imposed on top of the 10 per cent and 12.5 per cent tariffs introduced in July on a broader group of 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of anti-forced-labour laws.

Analysts said higher US trade barriers against China and other economies are the direction of travel, even if the Democratic Party - which won majorities in both houses of Congress earlier this month - tried to curb Trump's tariff impulses.

"Without the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto, Democrats' ability to dismantle the tariff wall will remain limited," ING analysts said in a note.

"Either way, we don't think the blue wave will mark a return to free trade. The Biden years already showed that tariffs in strategically important sectors enjoy support across political camps."

The US-China truce runs until Jan 10, but many expect it to be extended - potentially as early as next month when Trump and Xi are set to meet again at a Group of Twenty gathering in Miami - given the major impact a re-escalation of tit-for-tat hikes similar to those seen in 2025 would have on both economies.

The USTR's investigation is also partly directed at Chinese investment in Southeast Asian countries, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.

Commentary: Trump’s tariff wall isn’t going anywhere

items.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
items.summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
items.body:
Image source, REUTERS/Jane Rosenberg

Image caption,

Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.

ByRachel Clun

Business reporter

Updated 8 minutes ago

Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.

"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."

However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.

Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.

"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."

Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.

"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

BRUSSELS: The European Union (EU) announced on Wednesday (Nov 25) plans to earmark up to 50 billion euros (US$55 billion) to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe, as the bloc seeks to avoid losing further ground to the United States and China in advanced technologies.

The fund would "ensure access to innovative funding instruments, not only for quantum technologies, but more widely for all critical technologies which are necessary to our tech sovereignty and economic security," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told a press conference at the European parliament in Strasbourg.

"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now 50 billion euros," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point".

Both the rules and fund are part of the bloc's broader efforts to cut dependency on US and other non-European technologies.

Quantum technology harnesses the power of quantum mechanics - laws that govern how physics operates at atomic and sub-atomic scales - to solve certain problems much faster than traditional computers.

The EU expects the impact of quantum computing to be "catalytic" in several areas, leading to breakthroughs on drugs, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries. Quantum could even accelerate AI development.

The new rules will push public authorities to favour European businesses for public money over non-EU firms.

But Virkkunen said Europe remained open to working with "like-minded international partners" in the quantum field.

"This is not a blanket requirement that every component be manufactured in the EU," the European Commission said.

The law would be adopted after negotiations between EU states and parliament.

Europe says it wants to be a global leader in quantum computing by 2030.

The bloc is already a world leader in quantum research but lags in translating this into viable commercial opportunities.

"Our industrial ecosystem is fragile due to fragmented support across the member states and also lower access to private capital compared to USA and China," Virkkunen said.

Quantum start-ups in Europe currently attract only five per cent of global private funding compared to 50 per cent in the United States, she said.

The EU says future benefits from quantum advances could include more secure communications for military and national security operations, or helping to develop more advanced defence equipment.

Despite its potential, quantum technologies also pose cybersecurity risks, such as breaking encryption and other systems protecting digital data, at a time when AI and cyberattacks are rattling governments and companies.

The European Commission last week said an AI-assisted cyberattack hit its systems in October, which came after hacks on store freezers across Europe that resulted in huge losses of food.

items.title: Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
items.summary: The son of Zimbabwe's late former President Robert Mugabe has faced multiple legal troubles in the recent past.
items.body:
Image source, Gallo Images via Getty Images

Image caption,

Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe

ByBasillioh Rukanga

A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.

Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.

The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.

They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.

Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.

The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.

Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.

Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.

His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.

Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.

In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.

In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.

He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

items.title: Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
items.summary: Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, the US Coast Guard said.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByHarriet Whitehead

Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.

The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.

Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.

Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

items.title: Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect Earth
items.summary: The mission is studying an asteroid deliberately knocked off course by a colliding spacecraft.
items.body:
Image source, ESA

Image caption,

The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos

ByRebecca Morelle , Alison Francis and Tony Jolliffe, BBC News Science

A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.

It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.

The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

Image source, NASA/Johns Hopkins APL

Image caption,

This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022

The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.

Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.

"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.

"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."

Image source, NASA/Hubble Space Telescope

Image caption,

A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope

The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.

The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.

A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.

This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.

"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.

"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."

Image source, ESA

Image caption,

Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background

Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.

The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.

"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."

She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.

"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."

Image source, ESA

Image caption,

Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up close

Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.

A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.

There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.

Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.

But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.

This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

JAKARTA: Three people have died while search and rescue operations are currently underway for an "estimated" 23 more workers trapped in a mine in West Java province on Wednesday (Nov 25), authorities said.

The miners have been stuck in a mine 100m deep since Monday as heavy rains inundated access, the search and rescue agency said, adding access was narrow and the terrain was slippery and dark.

"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement.

The agency said the first body was recovered at 12.20pm (local time), followed by the second at 12.35pm and the third at 1.48pm.

The mine is located in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous area 60km south of the capital Jakarta.

State miner Antam, which operates gold mining operations in Pongkor, said the incident occurred at an unauthorised gold mine and was not a part of its operations.

Small-scale and illegal mining has often caused accidents in resource-rich Indonesia, where mineral resources are located in remote areas in conditions difficult for authorities to regulate.

JAKARTA: Three people have died while search and rescue operations are currently underway for an "estimated" 23 more workers trapped in a mine in West Java province on Wednesday (Nov 25), authorities said.
The miners have been stuck in a mine 100m deep since Monday as heavy rains inundated access, the search and rescue agency said, adding access was narrow and the terrain was slippery and dark.

"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement.
The agency said the first body was recovered at 12.20pm (local time), followed by the second at 12.35pm and the third at 1.48pm.

Australia, Solomon Islands sign sweeping pact stymieing China

The treaty cements Australia as the island nation's "primary security partner" and will see Canberra commit US$490 million over a decade to fund free education and other programmes.

CANBERRA: Solomon Islands and Australia signed a sweeping treaty on Wednesday (Nov 25), affirming there will be no foreign military base in the Pacific nation in a deal seen as a blow to China's ambitions in the region.

Prime Minister Matthew Wale and 15 ministers visited Canberra for talks spanning security, infrastructure, education and health.

"Solomon Islands has been for a number of years a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region," Wale told journalists alongside Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese.

"Those days are gone."

The treaty cements Australia as the island nation's "primary security partner" and will see Canberra commit AU$740 million ($490 million) over a decade to fund free education and other programs.

It affirms the "sovereign decision" by the Solomon Islands that there will be no foreign military or security base on its soil.

Solomon Islands' "sensitive" infrastructure will also "remain free from militarisation, foreign interference and unauthorised access".

The treaty text shows that will span airports, ports, energy and telecommunications - where China has built infrastructure under million-dollar loans since the country switched ties from Taiwan in 2019 - but the clause will not be applied retrospectively.

The Solomon Islands will also be required to consult with Australia before making deals with other countries on critical infrastructure or security cooperation outside members of the Pacific Islands Forum regional bloc, Albanese said.

He praised the deal as a "new chapter in our partnership to strengthen our shared prosperity and our security".

Wale has been in a diplomatic sprint since he was elected leader in May, upending close ties with Beijing built by predecessor Manasseh Sogavare and travelling to Canberra and Washington to rebuild relationships with traditional partners.

Asked about reports he had ended a secretive security pact with Beijing, Wale told journalists that discussions with China were "ongoing".

He could not comment further due to a non-disclosure clause in the deal.

China's foreign ministry on Tuesday said its ties with Pacific nations were not matters of "geopolitical contests".

Prime Minister of Solomon Islands Matthew Wale (left) and Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese after a signing ceremony in Parliament House in Canberra on Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Saeed Khan)

CHINA FEARS

Struck in 2022, the pact had "caught Canberra unprepared for a new era of intense geopolitical competition with China in Australia's immediate neighbourhood," Mihai Sora, director of research at the Lowy Institute think tank, said.

The Solomons hosted Chinese police and Australia grew anxious the deal also covered the Chinese navy.

The pact "made real the prospect of a persistent Chinese military presence some 1,600KM off the coast of Australia," Sora, a former Australian diplomat in the Solomons, told AFP.

It "was the catalyst for the past four years of frenetic Australian diplomacy in the region in an attempt to stem further strategic damage," he added.

Australia countered by striking security alliances or wide-ranging treaties with another five Pacific island countries.

Wale adjourned the Solomons parliament indefinitely in September after staring down a no-confidence vote.

He was forced to abruptly leave a Pacific leaders' summit in Palau to stop the attempt to bring down his new coalition government on the eve of a visit by the US Deputy Secretary of State.

Prime Minister of Solomon Islands Matthew Wale during a press conference in Canberra on Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Saeed Khan)

REFORMS EXPECTED

Solomons officials told AFP on Wednesday that parliament will return in January to approve significant reforms, including a pledge for free education.

A third of Solomon Islands children don't start school, and only 19 per cent finish because of the cost.

The Australian funds will be in place by January, bolstering Wale's government as parliament returns.

Over a decade, Australia will provide A$670 million in grants and A$70 million in concessional loans to boost education, health, policing, resources and climate resilience.

The treaty also covers road and bridge construction - areas China has dominated in the islands through its Belt and Road Initiative.

Wale said the decision to approve the Australian treaty was taken by his entire cabinet, many of whom had travelled to Canberra for the signing.

Solomons opposition party leader, Sogavare on Tuesday criticised the "fast-tracking" of the treaty with Australia while the status of China security arrangement remained "unclear".

Solomon Islands bars China and Taiwan from top Pacific summit

Commentary: Even those who don’t know Solomon Islands should take note of its security pact with China

items.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
items.summary: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
items.body:
Figure caption,

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

ByRachel Clun and Michael Race, Business reporters

US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.

In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

• Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone awayPublished8 hours ago

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.

Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".

Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

items.title: Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
items.summary: Solomon Islands leader Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics

ByHelen Davidson

Reporting fromSydney

The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.

At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".

In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing.

There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.

On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.

Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.

He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".

"Those days are done, gone," Wale said.

Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.

"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."

"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."

On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.

"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.

The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.

It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.

Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.

"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.

William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".

Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.

Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.

The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.

Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.

Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China.

This left motorists with an unusual choice: take a detour of nearly 20km, or pass briefly through Russian territory without a visa or border checks, provided they did not stop.

For a country sharing a roughly 340km border with Russia, the episode illustrates how even a tiny geographical anomaly can become a security concern amid heightened tensions between Moscow and the West.

“We've made changes to our training systems just to be more ready if some sort of crisis happens here,” said Renet Merdikes, head of the Saatse Border Guard Station, whose team patrols nearly a third of the border.

Estonian border guards patrol along the border with Russia near Saatse. (Image: CNA)

A barbed-wire fence along the border between Estonia and Russia. (Image: CNA)

A road leading into Russia is closed off at the Estonian side of the border. (Image: CNA)

In August, officials blamed Moscow for an arson attack on Tallinn-based Milrem Robotics, which manufactures unmanned vehicles, some of which have been deployed to Ukraine.

Moscow has denied involvement in the arson attacks and vowed to respond with political and diplomatic measures, accusing Tallinn of trying to ‌“erect a new Iron Curtain”.

“Estonia is pretty resilient about that, but my question is whether the other capitals in Europe are.”

During a visit to Estonia last month, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte sought to reassure allies that such incidents would not weaken the alliance's resolve.

“We will react when we need to react. The most important thing is to … stay calm, carry on, invest in defence,” he said.

He also reiterated the need to ensure Ukraine receives the military assistance it requires.

Across Europe, reports of suspicious drone activity near airports, military installations and other critical infrastructure have prompted governments to strengthen their counter-drone capabilities.

In Germany, authorities have linked Russia to suspected drone incidents at Leipzig/Halle Airport. In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes. The device reportedly failed to explode because of a faulty detonator.

“That increased threat has (made) all of us realise that we need to invest in counter-drone equipment to detect what's happening and also figure out ways to deal with it.”

Because much of continental Europe operates under the Schengen system, visas issued by one member state can generally allow travel across other participating countries, subject to applicable entry restrictions.

“It's not only a moral question on how you can let Russians go shopping in Paris when Ukrainians are dying every day,” Estonian Interior Minister Igor Taro told CNA.

“It's also a question about security because (Russia is) using these tourists – their citizens – for hybrid attacks.”

“He (Putin) miscalculated by a large scale. He thought Ukraine had nothing to fight with – no resources, no army. He thought the Ukrainians were not willing to fight. (Another) miscalculation was that he thought that no one would help,” Taro said.

“The biggest risk is that they (the Russians) can do it again. Obviously, Putin is not getting the real information from the frontline … or they would be out already. That's why they are still hoping to achieve something.”

RIYADH: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said on Wednesday (Nov 25) it had struck Yemen's Hodeida after the Iran-backed group threatened to retaliate against the kingdom's Red Sea ports if the attack took place.

The coalition, which support Yemen's internationally recognised government, renewed fighting in July against the Iran-backed fighters, who control swathes of the country, including Hodeida.

"We targeted operational capabilities at the port of Hodeidah," the Saudi-led coalition posted on X.

Riyadh had instructed civilians in Hodeida to evacuate in a social media post early on Wednesday.

The Houthi's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, had earlier threatened Saudi Arabia with retaliation in the event of an attack.

"The port of Jeddah, along with all other Saudi enemy ports along the Red Sea coast, will become targets for our forces should the enemy carry out its threats to bombard the port of Hodeidah," he posted on Telegram on Wednesday.

Saudi skyscraper hit again, coalition slams 'terrorist attack'

Houthi media outlet Almasirah reported an "attack on the port of Hodeida", without providing further details. No casualties or injuries have been reported.

Almasirah added that Saudi forces had also attacked the area's international airport.

Saree warned civilians near Saudi ports to "evacuate immediately and keep their distance" and called for "all shipping companies to remove their vessels from these ports at once".

The Saudi capital's tallest skyscraper was struck for a second time in days on Tuesday, wounding 11 people. The coalition called it a "terrorist attack" and blamed the strike on the Houthis.

Qatar and Pakistan, who have been acting as mediators in efforts to end the wider Middle East conflict between Iran and the United States both "strongly" condemned the attack on the tower, which houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund.

Two Indian citizens were wounded, the South Asian nation's foreign ministry said, adding such attacks "seriously endanger civilian lives, violate the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, and undermine regional security and stability."

The building had already been attacked last Thursday and is one of several high-profile targets hit since fighting with the Iran-backed group reignited in July.

Nvidia board joins Jensen Huang under scrutiny after reinstating embattled CEO

Nvidia’s board faces scrutiny after unanimously rehiring Jensen Huang days after accepting his resignation, fuelling calls for accountability and transparency.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs after a welcome ceremony with President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People, on May 14, 2026, in Beijing. (Photo: AP/Mark Schiefelbein)

NEW YORK: Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the company's board is joining him at the centre of scrutiny.

The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia's president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and "input from senior levels of the United States government". President Donald Trump said he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.

Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.

“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.

The board's stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump's role means for the meeting of business and politics.

CONCERNS SWIRL

Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the company and a group of more recent additions who have experience at big-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.

Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.

Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.

“The shareholders should demand a new board,” she said.

Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.

“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”

It’s not unusual for US tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.

American business has a culture of “leader heroes” - entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance".

Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang is back, but questions facing Nvidia remain, say analysts

Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.

“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”

The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window" if the sitting president "essentially tells them what to do," said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.

“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.

Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives" in their relationships with businesses.

LAWMAKERS CALL FOR ACCOUNTABILITY

The Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang's affair raised questions about Nvidia's compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervour on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.

Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and scepticism.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was "reckless". She wrote in a statement on Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board “still owe Congress answers".

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang's affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president's intervention "does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favour".

The California Department of Justice said on Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang said he violated code of conduct, source says

Commentary: Jensen Huang should never have been too big to fail at Nvidia

SOME MEMBERS JOINED NVIDIA BOARD IN 1990s

Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.

Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.

Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.

Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.
